name: Blood Pressure

yellow.text: Top number 121–139 or bottom 81–89 (high); top 86–99 or bottom 56–59 (low)

red.text: 140/90 or higher; 85/55 or lower; or any reading with fainting or chest pain

equipment: Strap or tether to hold the arm in place
steps: Rest quietly for a few minutes. Do not drink coffee or exercise first.
Fit the cuff on your bare upper arm and strap the arm at heart level so it does not float.
Press start, stay still and silent, then record both numbers.
when: Daily within 30 minutes of waking, before caffeine or exercise, and never within 45 minutes after an ARED workout.
mistakes: Measuring after coffee or exercise.
Measuring within 45 minutes of an ARED workout.
Letting the arm float away from heart level.
Talking or moving during the reading.
Comparing with Earth values only: your space baseline sits slightly lower.
escalate_if: The reading is Yellow or Red after a 30-minute seated rest and repeat.
Any dizziness, fainting or chest pain: tick the symptom checklist.
why: In weightlessness body fluid shifts toward the head and blood volume falls by 12–15%, so a healthy astronaut's blood pressure sits a little below Earth averages. Readings that drift out of your own band can mean volume loss or strain on the heart and vessels.
benefits: Spots dehydration or heart strain early.
Uses your adapted baseline, so normal space changes do not cause false alarms.
Pairs with resting heart rate on the same node.

yellow: Sit and rest for 30 minutes, then repeat the measurement.
Check resting heart rate (1A-ii) and hydration.
Follow the crew medical checklist for fluid loading if the reading is low.
red: Repeat after 30 minutes of seated rest.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer.
Avoid exertion and EVA until cleared.
Include the 7-day trend in the report packet.

name: Resting Heart Rate

red.text: Over 100 bpm at rest on 2 readings 10 minutes apart, under 40 bpm, or with symptoms

equipment: Pulse oximeter, wrist band or chest strap that shows heart rate
Same device as the blood pressure cuff if it reads pulse
steps: Stay seated or strapped in, relaxed and still, for a few minutes.
Start the reading with the cuff, band or strap.
Record the steady number, not the first one that appears.
when: Daily, at the same time as the waking blood pressure.
mistakes: Measuring right after movement or exercise.
Reading the first flicker of the display instead of the steady value.
Using the Earth range instead of your own baseline.
Skipping the second reading when the first is over 100.
escalate_if: Over 100 bpm on 2 readings 10 minutes apart.
Under 40 bpm.
Any fainting, chest pain or dizziness.
why: Heart rate shows how the heart is coping with fluid shifts and lower blood volume. A rise or a drop from your own baseline can signal dehydration, illness or stress on the autonomic nervous system.
benefits: Quick and non-invasive.
Cross-checks blood pressure and HRV.
Catches illness or dehydration early.

yellow: Rest 10 minutes, drink water and repeat.
Check blood pressure (1A-i) and temperature (2B-ii).
Measure twice a day until it returns to Green.
red: Repeat after 10 minutes of rest to confirm.
Stop strenuous work and EVA.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and send the trend in the report packet.

name: Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD)

earth_range.text: 4.2–5.0 mm (5.9 mm or more is abnormal on Earth)

red.text: 5.8 mm or more, or any new blurred vision or lasting headache

steps: Close the eye, cover it with gel and rest the probe gently on the eyelid. Do not press.
Find the optic nerve behind the eye and freeze the image in the axial plane.
Measure the width of the dark sheath exactly 3 mm behind the back of the eye, and record it.
when: Every 3 days (demo schedule). Repeat in 24 hours if Yellow.
mistakes: Pressing on the eyelid, which squeezes the sheath.
Measuring at the wrong distance behind the eye (it must be 3 mm).
Using the Earth cutoff of 5.9 mm: your space alert starts earlier.
Taking one reading and ignoring the trend.
escalate_if: 5.8 mm or more.
New blurred vision or a headache that does not go away.
Rising readings over several checks.
why: Without gravity, fluid and pressure build up around the head. The optic nerve sheath widens, and this can lead to Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). ONSD is a screening sign, not a diagnosis, so a high value needs an expert to review the images.
benefits: Early warning for vision-threatening pressure changes.
Lets the flight surgeon see the trend before symptoms start.
Prompts a check of cabin CO₂, which can make it worse.

yellow: Repeat the measurement in 24 hours.
Check cabin CO₂ (4A-ii).
Review headache and vision symptoms.
red: Remember ONSD is a screen, not a diagnosis.
Send the ultrasound and any eye images to the flight surgeon (store-and-forward).
Check cabin CO₂ (4A-ii).
Schedule lower-body negative pressure per the crew medical checklist.

name: 24-hour Urine Calcium

input.label: 24-hour urine calcium (typed from the lab result)

steps: Collect all urine for 24 hours in the collection container.
Run the sample on the analyzer and read the calcium result.
Type the value (mg/day) into the check-in.
when: Weekly as a full 24-hour test. A hydration strip can be checked daily.
mistakes: Missing a collection and under-counting.
Thinking a hydration strip photo measures calcium. It only shows hydration.
Starting the 24 hours at a different time than the log says.
escalate_if: Over 260 mg/day (Yellow) or over 300 mg/day (Red).
Flank pain, blood in urine or a lot less urine.
why: Bones lose calcium in weightlessness, and it passes out in the urine. Together with lower urine volume, this makes kidney stones more likely, which could be a mission-ending emergency far from Earth.
benefits: Tracks bone loss and stone risk.
Shows whether exercise and hydration are working.
Gives the flight surgeon numbers to adjust treatment.

yellow: Drink about 1 extra litre of water gradually over several hours.
Check ARED resistive exercise loading.
Review vitamin D and sodium intake (salt raises calcium loss).
Ask the flight surgeon whether treatment is needed.
red: Do all the Yellow steps.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and send the result to the flight surgeon.
Follow flight-surgeon direction on any treatment, such as potassium citrate.

name: Daily Radiation Dose Rate

yellow.text: Over 1.5 mSv/day (ISS and Moon) or over 2.5 mSv/day (deep space)

red.text: 5.0 mSv/day or more, or a rate over 3 times baseline within 1 hour (Solar Particle Event)

input.label: Dose rate (from the cabin or personal dosimeter)

steps: Open the radiation panel on the dashboard. No manual measurement is needed.
Read today's dose rate and compare it with the baseline for your environment.
If it spikes, check the hourly trend and follow the shelter steps.
when: Continuous. Check at every check-in, and hourly while Yellow.
mistakes: Using ISS numbers on a Moon or Mars mission (baselines differ).
Ignoring a fast hourly rise because the daily average looks fine.
Confusing absorbed dose with dose equivalent when reading raw data.
escalate_if: Any hourly spike over 3 times baseline.
5.0 mSv/day or more.
Nausea, vomiting or tiredness after a solar event.
why: Beyond Earth's magnetic shield, cosmic rays and solar storms raise radiation exposure. Daily dose shows whether you are in a normal region or a solar storm, and it feeds your career dose total.
benefits: Early warning of a solar storm.
Helps plan EVAs and shelter time.
Keeps total dose as low as reasonably achievable.

yellow: Check the hourly dose each hour.
Limit EVA and time in low-shielding areas.
Review the shelter plan.
red: Abort any EVA now.
Move everyone to the storm shelter (water-wall or polyethylene-lined quarters).
Stay there until proton flux drops.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and ground (if reachable).

name: Cumulative Career Dose

baseline.text: No personal baseline. Compare with the 600 mSv career limit

yellow.text: 50% of limit (300 mSv) or more, or projected end-of-mission total 75% (450 mSv) or more

red.text: 80% (480 mSv) or more, projected 100% (600 mSv), or one event over 250 mSv

steps: Open the career dose card. The software adds up your exposure automatically.
Read the total in mSv and the percent of the 600 mSv limit.
Check the projected end-of-mission total.
when: Continuous. Review at each check-in and when planning EVAs.
mistakes: Forgetting dose from earlier flights.
Reading only the current total and not the projection.
Counting medical imaging in the career total (it is tracked separately).
escalate_if: Total reaches 50% or the projection reaches 75%.
A single event delivers over 250 mSv.
why: NASA sets a career limit of 600 mSv for all astronauts to keep cancer risk below an agreed level. Tracking the running total and the projection lets the crew change plans before the limit is at risk.
benefits: Keeps exposure within the standard.
Supports EVA and shielding decisions.
Shows if the mission plan needs to change.

yellow: Re-plan EVAs and shielding use.
Review the end-of-mission projection with the flight surgeon.
red: Re-plan EVAs and shielding immediately.
Limit time outside shelter.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and mission control.

name: White Blood Cell Count (WBC)

red.text: Under 3.5 (low white cells) or over 11.0 (high white cells)

steps: Wash and dry your hands, then prick the side of a fingertip.
Load the drop into the cartridge and place it in the analyzer.
Wait for the result and record the WBC number.
when: Weekly. Repeat right after any solar particle event or any fever of 38.0 °C or more.
mistakes: Squeezing the finger hard, which dilutes the sample.
Using too little blood.
Skipping the repeat after a solar event or fever.
escalate_if: Under 3.5 or over 11.0.
Fever of 38.0 °C or more together with a low or high count.
why: Radiation and stress weaken the immune system in space. A low count can mean bone-marrow suppression, and a high count can mean infection or inflammation. Dormant viruses such as shingles can also wake up.
benefits: Early sign of radiation effects.
Early sign of infection.
Works with temperature and skin checks.

yellow: Repeat the test after a solar event or fever.
Check temperature (2B-ii) and skin (4B-ii).
Watch for infection symptoms.
red: Repeat the test to confirm.
Check temperature and skin for shingles-type rash.
Wear a mask and limit close contact in the cabin.
Ask the Crew Medical Officer about antiviral or antibiotic treatment per the crew medical checklist.

name: Body Temperature

baseline.text: 37.1 ± 0.2 °C (typical 36.8–37.5; it runs a little higher in space)

steps: Wait 15 minutes after eating, drinking or exercise.
Place the thermometer correctly (under the tongue, or on the temple) and hold still.
Wait for the beep and record the temperature.
when: Daily. Twice a day while Yellow or unwell, and recheck in 1 hour if Red.
mistakes: Measuring right after a hot drink or exercise.
Poor probe placement.
Using the Earth range: your space baseline is slightly higher.
escalate_if: 38.0 °C or more.
Fever with a rash, cough or low white cell count.
why: In space, body heat is not carried away as easily and sleep cycles shift, so normal temperature runs a little higher. A real fever can point to infection, which is more likely when immunity is lowered.
benefits: Early sign of infection.
Supports the WBC and skin checks.
Quick and cheap.

yellow: Measure twice a day.
Rest and drink fluids.
Check WBC (2B-i) and skin (4B-ii).
red: Recheck in 1 hour.
Check WBC and skin (for shingles-type rash).
Wear a mask and limit close contact.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer; follow the crew medical checklist for treatment.

name: Sleep Duration

yellow.text: < 5.5 h (≤ 6.0 h is linked to slower psychomotor speed)

red.text: < 4.5 h for 2 or more nights in a row

equipment: Tablet or laptop for the sync
steps: Wear the actigraphy band snugly on the same wrist all night, including during short wake-ups.
In the morning, sync the band and read the total time asleep (not time in bed).
Enter or confirm that number in the daily check-in.
when: Every night. The band syncs automatically; confirm the value at the morning check-in.
mistakes: Counting time in bed instead of time actually asleep.
Taking the band off or charging it during the night.
Forgetting to sync, so the night shows as missing.
Judging sleep by how rested you feel: sleep-restricted crew often cannot tell they are impaired.
escalate_if: Sleep is under 5.5 h (Yellow).
Sleep is under 4.5 h on 2 nights in a row (Red).
You feel drowsy or make errors during a safety-critical task (docking, robotics, EVA).
why: Astronauts average only about 6.0–6.6 hours of sleep in flight. At 6 hours or less, NASA studies link sleep with slower reaction speed, more stress and attention lapses. Sleep-deprived crew also find it hard to notice their own decline, so an objective number is needed.
benefits: Catches sleep debt early, before it becomes normal.
Protects safety-critical work such as robotic arm use, docking and EVA.
Supports the PVT, mood and HRV checks on the same Brain node.

yellow: Protect one uninterrupted 8-hour sleep block tonight.
Dim the lights in the evening.
Stop caffeine late in the day.
Repeat the PVT-lite test after waking.
red: Postpone safety-critical tasks: robotic arm, docking and EVA.
Use blue-enriched morning light.
Contact the Crew Medical Officer. Any sleep medication only per crew medical checklist / flight-surgeon direction.
Schedule recovery sleep before returning to critical duties.

name: Psychomotor Vigilance (PVT-lite)

yellow.text: 291–350 ms, or 1 lapse (a response over 500 ms)

red.text: > 350 ms, or 2 or more lapses (responses over 500 ms)

equipment: Tablet or laptop running the PVT-lite test
A quiet spot where you will not be interrupted
steps: Sit still in a quiet place with one finger ready on the screen or mouse.
Press Start. In each of 5 trials, wait for the circle to turn green, then tap it as fast as you can.
Read the median time and the lapse count. They are sent to the check-in automatically.
when: Every day at the check-in, and again right before safety-critical tasks (docking, robotics, EVA).
mistakes: Tapping before the circle turns green. The trial repeats, so wait for green.
Taking the test while distracted or while talking to someone.
Testing within 2–4 hours of waking up, when sleep inertia slows reactions.
Switching devices or hands between days, which changes the numbers.
Treating it as a diagnosis. PVT-lite is a quick screening test only.
escalate_if: The result is still Yellow or Red after a 10-minute rest and a repeat test.
You have 2 or more lapses.
You feel foggy or drowsy before a safety-critical task, even if the result looks fine.
why: Sleep-deprived crew often cannot judge their own alertness. A short reaction test gives an objective number. On the ISS, the same kind of test shows slower reactions and more lapses when sleep is short or the body clock is out of step. Anyone still in Yellow or Red after a 10-minute rest is treated as fatigue-impaired.
benefits: Gives a quick, objective check of alertness before risky work.
Flags fatigue that you may not feel yourself.
Works together with the sleep, mood and HRV checks on the Brain node.

yellow: Rest for 10 minutes, then repeat the test.
Check last night's sleep (3A-i) for a cause.
If it is still Yellow, do not start safety-critical tasks until it clears.
red: Stop or postpone safety-critical tasks: docking, robotic arm and EVA.
Rest for 10 minutes and repeat the test once.
If it is still Red, you are fatigue-impaired: tell the Crew Medical Officer and ask a crewmate to cover your duties.
Review sleep (3A-i), mood (3B-i) and HRV (3B-ii) for linked changes.

name: Mood / Stress Score

red.text: 7 or higher, or any thoughts of self-harm

equipment: Check-in form or slider on the tablet
steps: Take a moment and think about how tense or stressed you feel right now.
Pick a number from 1 (calm) to 10 (very stressed).
Enter it in the check-in. Go with your first honest answer.
when: Daily at the routine check-in. Add a mid-day check if the score is Yellow.
mistakes: Giving the number you think is expected instead of the honest one.
Rating the whole week instead of how you feel today.
Skipping the check-in on busy days, when stress is often highest.
Ignoring a slow rise over several days because each day looks small.
escalate_if: The score is 7 or higher.
You have any thoughts of harming yourself: tell the Crew Medical Officer or a crewmate right away.
Stress keeps rising over several days, even if it is still Green.
why: On 6-month ISS missions, self-reported stress rises over time and is highest in the last quarter of flight. Stress also links to poor sleep and slower reactions. A simple daily number lets the crew notice the climb early.
benefits: Spots a slow build-up of stress before it affects teamwork or safety.
Takes under 10 seconds to log.
Gives behavioral health staff or the CMO a trend to act on.

yellow: Take a 10-minute mindfulness or breathing break.
Send a message to family or talk with a crewmate.
Do an extra mid-day check-in.
red: Contact the Crew Medical Officer now.
Book a private psychological conference with the ground behavioral health team. If the radio delay is long, use the offline coping protocol (guided breathing and virtual nature break).
Take 45 minutes of protected downtime.
Check sleep (3A-i), PVT (3A-ii) and HRV (3B-ii) for linked changes.

name: Heart Rate Variability (RMSSD)

baseline.text: 50 ± 4 ms (your own anchor matters more than the Earth range)

yellow.text: 42 ms or less (2 or more SD below your baseline, about a 15–25% drop)

red.text: 38 ms or less (3 or more SD below your baseline, over a 25% drop)

equipment: Chest strap ECG or wrist pulse sensor (PPG)
Tablet or app that reads RMSSD
steps: Rest quietly for about 5 minutes in the same position you always use. Stay still and breathe normally.
Wear the chest strap (moisten the electrodes) or a snug wrist band, then start the HRV reading without talking or moving.
Write down the RMSSD value in milliseconds when the reading ends.
when: Daily at rest, at the same time and in the same position each morning.
mistakes: Measuring right after exercise or caffeine.
Talking, moving or checking messages during the reading.
A loose strap or wrist band that gives noisy data.
Changing time or posture between days, which makes the trend meaningless.
Comparing your number with another person's or the Earth range instead of your own baseline.
escalate_if: The value stays Yellow or Red the next morning under the same conditions.
A low HRV comes with a high resting heart rate, poor sleep or high stress.
You feel unwell, dizzy or have chest pain. Tick the symptom checklist.
why: HRV shows how well the body recovers from strain. Normal values differ a lot between people, so the system compares you only with your own fixed baseline. A clear drop means the body is under load and not recovering well.
benefits: Gives an early sign of overload before you feel it.
Fair for every crew member, because it uses a personal baseline.
Helps explain changes in sleep, mood and reaction time.

yellow: Repeat the measurement next morning in identical resting conditions.
Check last night's sleep (3A-i) and today's stress (3B-i).
Plan lighter workload and good rest today.
red: Rest, then repeat the measurement to rule out a poor reading.
Reduce workload and avoid safety-critical tasks until it recovers.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and send the 7-day trend in the report packet.
Check resting heart rate (1A-ii), sleep (3A-i) and mood (3B-i) for linked changes.

name: Blood Oxygen (SpO₂)
steps: Warm your hand and remove any nail polish.
Clip the oximeter on a fingertip and keep the hand still at heart level.
Wait until the number is steady and record it.
when: Daily. Twice a day while Yellow; recheck in 5 minutes and check cabin O₂/CO₂.
mistakes: Cold fingers, which give a falsely low number.
Nail polish or a loose clip.
Moving the hand during the reading.
Writing down the first number before it settles.
escalate_if: 91% or lower.
Below 90% (supplemental oxygen is needed).
Shortness of breath, confusion or blue lips.
why: SpO₂ shows how well the lungs move oxygen into the blood. A drop can come from a cabin leak, low oxygen, a rising CO₂ level or a lung problem.
benefits: Fast and painless.
Catches cabin air problems early.
Backs up the cabin CO₂ reading on the same node.

yellow: Warm your hand and recheck in 5 minutes.
Check cabin O₂ and CO₂ displays.
Turn on ventilation fans.
Measure twice a day until Green.
red: Recheck right away.
Check cabin O₂/CO₂ and turn on fans.
If it is below 90%, give supplemental oxygen per the crew medical checklist.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer.

name: Cabin CO₂ Pressure (ppCO₂)
steps: Open the cabin air panel. The sensor reports automatically.
Read the current ppCO₂ and the 7-day average.
If it is rising, check fans and the CO₂ scrubber.
mistakes: Reading only the average and missing local pockets of CO₂ around your face.
Ignoring headaches that appear before the alarm.
Sleeping or working in a dead-air spot with no airflow.
escalate_if: 3.0 mm Hg or more.
Headache, tiredness, blurred vision or nausea.
why: In weightlessness, exhaled CO₂ does not rise away from your face. CO₂ also widens blood vessels in the brain, which adds to pressure behind the eyes. Astronauts feel symptoms at much lower CO₂ than people on Earth.
benefits: Protects thinking and vision.
Helps explain headaches and high ONSD.
Shows if the scrubber needs attention.

yellow: Switch on personal ventilation fans.
Move to a lower-CO₂ module.
Reduce hard physical effort.
Check the CO₂ removal system.
red: Do all the Yellow steps now.
Inspect the CO₂ removal system (CDRA) and sorbent beds.
Check ONSD (1B-i) and SpO₂ (4A-i).
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and ground (if reachable).

name: Fasting Blood Glucose

baseline.text: 90 ± 8 mg/dL (typical 75–105; insulin resistance is common in space)

steps: Measure in the morning after at least 8 hours without food. Wash and dry your hands.
Prick the side of a fingertip and touch the drop to the test strip.
Wait for the result and record the number.
when: Weekly in the morning, fasting. Daily while Yellow or Red; recheck in 15 minutes if low (under 70).
mistakes: Measuring after eating or drinking anything but water.
Wet or sugary fingers.
Using an expired strip.
Treating a low and a high result the same way.
escalate_if: 126 mg/dL or more.
Under 70 mg/dL.
Confusion, shaking or sweating, which can mean low glucose.
why: Without gravity and normal exercise load, the body can become less sensitive to insulin. A creeping rise shows early. A low reading is an emergency of its own, which is why the steps for high and low are different.
benefits: Early sign of insulin resistance.
Avoids treating low glucose the wrong way.
Gives the flight surgeon a 7-day trend.

yellow: Measure daily until it returns to Green.
Cut back on simple sugars.
Keep up ARED and aerobic exercise.
red_high: Repeat the fasting test tomorrow morning.
Keep up ARED and aerobic exercise.
Send the 7-day trend to the flight surgeon.
red_low: Take 15 g of fast carbohydrate now (glucose tablets or fruit juice).
Recheck in 15 minutes and repeat the carbohydrate if still under 70.
If you are confused or unresponsive, a crewmate starts emergency care and gives nothing by mouth.

name: Skin Status

yellow.text: 1–2: small mild rash, contact dermatitis or lunar-dust irritation

red.text: 3: spreading, blistering or painful rash (such as shingles), or any rash with fever

steps: Look over your skin, especially hands, arms, neck and any area touched by suit or dust.
Take a clear photo of any rash or change, in good light, with a size reference.
Pick the category (0–3) that fits best and record it.
when: Weekly. Take a photo daily while Yellow or Red.
mistakes: Photos in poor light or out of focus.
Ignoring a small rash that is spreading.
Forgetting to check temperature when there is a rash.
escalate_if: Category 3.
Any rash together with a fever.
A painful, one-sided or blistering rash.
why: Closed habitats have floating dust and mould, and lunar or Mars dust irritates skin. A weaker immune system in space can also wake up dormant viruses that show up as a rash, such as shingles.
benefits: Catches infection or irritation early.
Photos let the flight surgeon help from a distance.
Links to the WBC and temperature checks.

yellow: Wash gently and moisturise.
Take a photo each day.
Vacuum the habitat with the HEPA filter.
Check temperature (2B-ii).
red: Take clear photos and send them to the flight surgeon at once (store-and-forward).
Check temperature (2B-ii) and WBC (2B-i).
Do not start any treatment until authorized per the crew medical checklist.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer.

name: One-way Communication Delay

baseline.text: ISS about 0 s (A0); Moon about 1.3 s (A0); Mars 4–22 min (A2)

red.text: A2 Autonomous: over 5 min (turns on Earth-independent triage mode)

steps: Look at the banner at the top of the dashboard. It updates automatically.
Read the delay and the autonomy level (A0, A1 or A2).
At A2, open the offline triage checklist before acting.
mistakes: Waiting for ground answers when the delay makes that impractical.
Forgetting that messages and photos are queued, not instant.
escalate_if: The level changes to A2.
A communication blackout starts.
why: Near Earth, doctors on the ground can help in real time. On Mars the delay can be 4–22 minutes each way, so the crew must be able to triage and treat on their own. This indicator only sets the mode; it is never scored as a body measure.
benefits: Switches the app to the right mode automatically.
Shows when offline checklists are needed.
Applies the 10-point penalty only when a Red indicator exists at A2.

yellow: Expect delayed replies and plan ahead.
Send complete reports in one message.
red: Use the offline Crew Medical Officer checklist.
Package the report for ground to be sent when the link allows.
Do not wait for ground approval on urgent steps in the checklist.

name: Medical Kit Stock

red.text: Under 50%, or any life-critical item used up (oxygen, IV fluid, key drug)

steps: Open the medical kit card. The inventory updates when items are used.
Read the percent remaining and any life-critical items that are low.
Log every item you use so the count stays correct.
when: Continuous, updated whenever an item is dispensed.
mistakes: Using an item and forgetting to log it.
Looking only at the total and missing a life-critical item that is nearly gone.
escalate_if: Under 70%.
Under 50%.
Any life-critical item is depleted.
why: On a long mission there is no resupply and no quick return to Earth. Knowing what is left decides which treatments are possible. This is context for the crew and does not change the health score.
benefits: Prompts early conservation.
Helps choose treatments you can actually deliver.
Gives ground a clear stock picture.

yellow: Start conservation steps.
Use checklist-approved alternatives where possible.
red: Follow the conservation protocol strictly.
Use only checklist-approved alternatives.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and report to ground.
